source_refs.note: Topic 11.2.2, printed pages 247-249. The printed structural drawings are described by name.

blocks.text: Branched-chain alkanes are named by the following rules.

items: Locate the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms; it determines the parent name. A compound whose longest chain has six carbons is a hexane even if the chain is bent; the longest chain may not be obvious from the way the formula is written, and a compound is a heptane if its longest chain has seven carbons.
Number the longest chain from the end nearest the substituent.
Use the numbers from rule 2 to give the location of the substituent: the parent name is placed last and the substituent, preceded by its number, first (for example 2-methylhexane).

With two or more substituents, give each a number for its position on the longest chain, for example 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane. List the substituents alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), ignoring multiplying prefixes such as di and tri.
When two substituents are on the same carbon atom, use that number twice.
When two or more substituents are identical, use the prefixes di, tri, tetra and so on, and make certain that every substituent has a number.
When two chains of equal length compete as the parent chain, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents.
When branching first occurs at an equal distance from either end of the longest chain, choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference.

blocks.alt: Two condensed formulae with the longest carbon chain shaded blue and the substituent CH3 circled in pink. First: H3C-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3, a straight six-carbon chain with CH3 on the fifth carbon. Second: H3C-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH(-CH3) whose shaded chain turns down through CH2 and CH3, seven carbons, with the circled CH3 to the right.
blocks.caption: Rule 1 examples: the longest continuous chain (a hexane and a heptane) (original drawing after the scheme printed on p247 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: The same two compounds with carbon numbers. The bent heptane chain is numbered 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 along the top and 2, 1 down the bend, so the circled CH3 is on carbon 3; an arrow labels it Substituent. The hexane chain is numbered 6 to 1 from left to right, so the circled CH3 hangs from carbon 2; an arrow labels it Substituent.
blocks.caption: Rule 2 examples: numbering from the end nearest the substituent (original drawing after the scheme printed on p247 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: The numbered, shaded chains with names: the bent seven-carbon chain with the circled CH3 on carbon 3 is 3-methylheptane; the straight six-carbon chain with the circled CH3 on carbon 2 is 2-methylhexane.
blocks.caption: Rule 3 examples: 3-methylheptane and 2-methylhexane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p248 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Shaded chain H3C-CH-CH2-CH-CH2-CH3 numbered 1 to 6. A circled CH3 hangs from carbon 2 and a circled CH2 joined to a circled CH3 (an ethyl group) hangs from carbon 4. Name: 4-Ethyl-2-methylhexane.
blocks.caption: Rule 4 example: 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p248 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Chain H3C-CH2-C-CH2-CH2-CH3 numbered 1 to 6. Carbon 3 carries a CH3 above and a CH2-CH3 (ethyl) below. Name: 3-Ethyl-3-methylhexane.
blocks.caption: Rule 5 example: 3-ethyl-3-methylhexane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p248 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Three condensed formulae. H3C-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3, 2,3-Dimethylbutane. H3C-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3 with the middle CH3 drawn above, 2,3,4-Trimethylpentane. H3C-C(CH3)2-C(CH3)2-CH3 with two methyls above and below each central carbon, 2,2,3,3-Tetramethylbutane.
blocks.caption: Rule 6 examples: 2,3-dimethylbutane, 2,3,4-trimethylpentane and 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p248 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Chain H3C-CH2-CH-CH-CH-CH-CH3 numbered 7 to 1 from left to right. CH3 groups hang from carbons 5, 3 and 2, and a propyl chain CH2-CH2-CH3 hangs from carbon 4. Name: 2,3,5-Trimethyl-4-propylheptane.
blocks.caption: Rule 7 example: 2,3,5-trimethyl-4-propylheptane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p249 of the textbook).

blocks.alt: Chain CH3-CH-CH2-CH-CH-CH3 numbered 6 to 1 from left to right, with CH3 groups on carbons 5, 3 and 2. Name: 2,3,5-Trimethylhexane (not 2,4,5-trimethylhexane).
blocks.caption: Rule 8 example: 2,3,5-trimethylhexane (original drawing after the scheme printed on p249 of the textbook).
